projectTitle: ENCORE - Engineered Nanocompartments for Capture, Optimization and Reactor Engineering
tagline: A standardized modular Golden Gate toolkit that expresses self-assembling encapsulin nanocompartments with custom cargo in yeast
summary: KIT, the first iGEM team at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, built ENCORE: a standardised modular cloning system (the toolKIT) that co-expresses a self-assembling encapsulin protein nanocompartment and its cargo in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, chosen because encapsulins assemble from a single repeating subunit and so need far fewer transcriptional units than bacterial microcompartments or virus-like particles. They won the 2026 Inclusivity Award for work that turned inward rather than outward: instead of role-model campaigns, they asked how tasks are actually distributed inside scientific teams and what role gender plays, surveyed 71 people, ran proper statistics, and published the negative result honestly. The resulting deliverables - a facilitated workshop with moderation guide and printable worksheet, and TeamKIT, a team-and-meeting-culture guide - are the reusable artefacts.

dry.frameworks: Survey research methodology applied with unusual rigour for an iGEM team: seven self-derived teamwork task categories (Coordination, Social, Operational, Scientific Conception, Creative Design, External Communication, Leadership/Mentoring) each with a written definition; separation of actual task distribution from perceived distribution; a 12-item five-point Likert instrument grouped into three constructs (Perception, Autonomy, Allocation) of four items each with one reverse-scored item; debriefing placed deliberately at the end of the instrument so as not to prime respondents, following social-science practice; expert instrument review; piloting; and an ethics-committee determination.
dry.dataviz: A heptagon dot-poster used as the physical pre-survey instrument at Campus Day, later rebuilt as an interactive clickable heptagon on the wiki; grouped mean-frequency bar charts of task distribution by gender for the full dataset and the iGEM subgroup; box plots of Likert sum scores for Perception, Autonomy and Allocation; diverging stacked bar charts of each Likert item by gender with sub-10% segments suppressed; an interactive TeamKIT map where a visitor picks their chapter and situation and is pointed to a model and an exercise; and a self-check tool so a reader can see which roles they take in their own team. Figures were generated with AI assistance (Claude) and labelled as such.
dry.datascience: Pre-survey n = 58 (30 female, 28 male) at KIT Campus Day; main survey n = 71 (45 female, 24 male, 2 non-binary, the latter excluded from gender comparison for sample size and stated as a limitation), of whom 59 were iGEM members, 8 from research groups and 4 from university groups, predominantly undergraduate (41) and graduate (18) students. Because the data were not normally distributed the team used two-sample Mann-Whitney U tests rather than Welch t-tests, at alpha = 0.05. Result: for every task area the null hypothesis held, except Scientific Conception in the full dataset (p = 0.039), where men reported taking it on more often; that difference vanished in the iGEM-only subgroup. All three Likert constructs showed no significant gender difference (p = 0.271, 0.750, 0.113) and scale reliability was good to excellent (Cronbach's alpha 0.822, 0.991, 0.930). The single most striking descriptive finding: for 'I receive adequate recognition for my contributions to the team', no male participant disagreed while 9 of 45 women did. Limitations are set out at length - voluntary-participation selection bias, no cultural-background data collected, comparability of iGEM teams with research groups uncertain, no participant reported being in a predominantly male team despite ~70% of KIT students being male, and the team states plainly it has no formal social-science training.
dry.software: Two integrated tools. The Open NC Database curates nanocompartment properties scattered across the primary literature - internal volume, pore diameter and charge, reported stability, associated targeting peptide - into a searchable, filterable form, with a data model that distinguishes the biological candidate from the experimentally reported assembly and its supporting evidence and explicitly marks unreported values as unreported; candidates are keyed by UniProt accession and structures by PDB identifier, a sequence enters the catalog only after a documented translation check, and the database accepts contributions by pull request. The ENCORE-Builder turns a database selection into a complete Golden Gate / MoClo design: it assigns fusion sites across three cloning levels, places start and stop codons, codon-optimises for S. cerevisiae, designs primers and oligonucleotide pairs, avoids sites forbidden by RFC 10 and RFC 1000, and emits annotated GenBank and SBOL 3 files plus order lists, with the toolKIT's combinatorial rules enforced so invalid designs cannot be produced. It was validated against a real cloning: the Builder's Level 2 design for the Quasibacillus thermotolerans shell with LGB4 matches the construct the team cloned in the lab.

techniques: encapsulin shell self-assembly in S. cerevisiae

good.publicEngagement: KIT won Inclusivity by doing what almost no previous iGEM gender-equity project had done: looking inward. The team read the iGEM Diversity & Inclusion Committee blog post 'Bursting demographic bubbles', surveyed prior iGEM work (Paris Bettencourt 2013, JIASHU-Shanghai 2024, Stony Brook 2022, Patras-Med 2024, Guelph 2024) and identified that almost all of it faces outward through role models, outreach to girls or awareness campaigns, with only Guelph coming close to an internal view by surveying its own composition. KIT's research question went further: not who is on the team, but how work is distributed - who ends up in the lab, who presents, who takes the organisational and invisible tasks, and, memorably, who empties the dishwasher in the institute kitchen. They derived seven task categories from reflecting on their own team, tested them as a physical heptagon dot-poster at KIT Campus Day (n = 58, colour-coded dots by gender), then designed a full instrument separating actual task distribution from perception, had it reviewed by Dr Melanie-Marita Leidecker-Sandmann of KIT's Department of Science Communication (who had them shorten items, add demographics, remove two questions that revealed the hypothesis, and add a proper debriefing), piloted it with Engineers Without Borders at KIT, obtained an ethics-committee determination, and distributed it through Instagram, the official iGEM Slack and a QR-code flyer at the Barcelona Meetup, plus KIT mailing lists. 71 responses came back. The honest headline is that their hypothesis was not supported - women did not take disproportionately more secretarial or communication work - but two findings held: most participants of either gender agreed organisational work receives less recognition than research work, and 9 of 45 women versus 0 of 24 men felt their contributions were not adequately recognised. They published the full statistics, the Cronbach's alphas, the raw data, both survey versions and the ethics statement, and wrote a long, specific limitations section. The transfer step is what makes this copyable. After discussing results with Ines Koehler, Head of KIT's Department for Equal Opportunities and Diversity Management, who invoked iGEM's 'give back to the community' principle, the team built two artefacts. The Gender Roles & Task Distribution Workshop is designed for newly formed teams at the start of collaboration, when patterns are easiest to shift: each person maps how their time splits across the seven task areas and rates satisfaction with each, then in paired conversations talks to someone who regularly carries a task area they themselves would feel least confident taking on, making invisible effort tangible; it ends with concrete next steps including a weekly challenge where members swap tasks and a check-in a few weeks later. The full moderation guide with a printable worksheet is downloadable, needs no prior gender-research knowledge, and adapts to 1.5-2.5 hour sessions. It was revised after written feedback from Ines Koehler and from Anietta Weckauff and Marina Jaehnert Giannitrapani, co-founders of the Women in STEM Initiative at the University of Stuttgart - changes included replacing 'blind spot' with 'perception gap' because unnoticed tasks are not wilfully ignored, changing 'a task I would never do' to 'a task area you feel least confident taking on' so the choice does not read as a judgment of the task's worth, adding a satisfaction rating, explicit ground rules, an opt-out in the warm-up, a note on intersectional factors and a recommendation for mixed-gender co-moderation. The team states plainly that neither version has been piloted yet and asks teams who run it to report back. TeamKIT is a downloadable guide to team and meeting culture built because, as the first KIT team with no predecessor, they had to work out task distribution, meetings and conflict from nothing - and found first-year teams at Aarhus and Berlin had the same problem; it moves from individual strengths and interests through interpersonal communication to the whole team, ending with meeting and conflict methods, with inclusion threaded through rather than placed in its own chapter, and it was reviewed by Freja from iGEM Aarhus. Public outreach for a Foundational Advance project was equally deliberate, since nanocompartments are invisible and hard to picture. Three members joined KIT's first science slam camp, eight workshop days on storytelling, stage presence, visualisation and PR, and performed to around 100 people at a Karlsruhe science communication event with a metaphor they arrived at only after scrapping draft after draft: the yeast cell is a ball pit and the nanocompartment a wonder machine that fetches a toy you are too big to reach, gives a child a protected space to make chewing gum without harming anything around it, and takes snapshots of children quarrelling among the balls (mRNA capture). CoLab was an art exhibition built on an open call that asked artists a question rather than commissioning illustrations: what becomes of a promoter, what could competent cells be, what does autoclaving mean, and what do you see in four unlabelled scientific figures from the team's own lab work; eleven works by nine artists (one dating from 1980) were shown over two weekends in October at the pavilions in the Fasanengarten in Karlsruhe with team members present throughout, and visitors asked questions that never come up in the lab - what exactly are you changing in those cells, what happens to them afterward, who decides what is allowed. 'The Yeast We Can Do' is a fully open board game for 3-6 players aged 12+, about 45 minutes, no prior knowledge needed, with 19 missions across six application areas from breaking down forever chemicals to capturing CO2 and growing nanocrystals, where all players compete for the same 20 amino acids on the same 37 fields of nutrient medium; rules, board image, mission cards, event cards, score pad and quick reference are downloadable PDFs and the yeast-cell and budding-yeast playing pieces are STL files for any FDM printer, all on GitLab. The team's stated design goal is that a complete newcomer leaves knowing a protein is a chain of twenty kinds of beads, some hard to come by, while an iGEMer might spot the catalytic triad in the plastic-degrading enzyme. They also ran two pub quizzes at the student-run venue Z10 (27 April and again on 15 October during first-year orientation week), staffed a Campus Day stand with a science quiz, a pipette-tip-box filling race and pipetting lessons, published ENCORE in BIOspektrum 04/26 (a leading German molecular life sciences journal, Springer Nature) and in the KIT student magazine clicKIT, built a social media identity from zero deliberately as team-building infrastructure for their successors, and hosted the first iGEM Baden-Wuerttemberg Meetup at KIT on 13 June with GU Frankfurt, Bonn, Saarland, Aachen, Berlin, Heidelberg and Stuttgart, opening with a poster-design session by Sylvia Erhardt of the Center for Synthetic Genomics and continuing with a peer-consultation workshop where teams brought their most pressing internal problems and bottlenecks for structured peer feedback, including team-dynamics questions that rarely surface in formal settings. The wiki itself is an accessibility deliverable, built following UniMuenster 2023's 'Inclusive Wiki Design' guide: large clear sans-serif type, a high-contrast palette of six colours in three shades each chosen for colour-vision deficiency, one-click OpenDyslexic font toggle, one-click dark mode, descriptive alt text on every figure for screen readers, a glossary of scientific terms and abbreviations, a site-wide search function, and shape-coded navigation (encapsulin-shaped octagons for research, circles for Human Practices) so section is distinguishable without relying on colour. Commitments extend past the competition: gender-specific task distribution may feature in next year's KIT Diversity Day, and an article about the project will appear in the KIT Diversity Magazine.
good.ihp: Integrated Human Practices is tightly coupled to the inclusivity work - the interview with Ines Koehler of KIT's Equal Opportunities and Diversity Management department is documented on the iHP page and is what converted the survey from a finding into two deliverables. The survey's own development through expert feedback, piloting and revision is itself documented as an engineering cycle ('Survey on Task Distribution') on the Engineering page, applying DBTL to a social-science instrument. The team explicitly anchored the work to UN Sustainable Development Goal 5 (gender equality) and to the local fact that roughly 70% of KIT students in engineering and technical programmes are male, while in Europe only one in five ICT and engineering specialists is female.
good.realWorld: Everything is downloadable and reusable: the workshop moderation guide and printable worksheet, the TeamKIT guide, the full board game (rules, board, cards, score pad, quick reference, STL print files) on GitLab, both survey versions, the raw data and the ethics statement, the Open NC Database (open to pull requests) and the ENCORE-Builder (new parts, adapters and backbones added as data files so other teams can extend it). The team's framing of why this matters for successors is worth copying: 'fair task distribution should not depend on whether a team happens to have someone who already cares about the topic', and the most useful thing a first team can leave behind is not a project but a starting point.

gemsTakeaway: Point inclusivity work at your own house before the public: survey how tasks are actually distributed inside your own teams with a properly reviewed instrument, publish the result even when it contradicts your hypothesis, and convert it into a ready-to-run workshop plus a team-culture guide that a brand-new cohort can use in week one, so fair task distribution does not depend on one person happening to care.
